title: Printing integers and characters
summary: Match each printf format specifier to a value in the right argument register, at the width the specifier expects.

body.markdown:
Read these first:

- [Printing a string with printf](/learn/printing-strings-hello-world)
Printing an integer takes one step more than printing a string: the format string names a type, and the value goes in the next argument register.

In the C programming language, printing different data types is accomplished by providing the appropriate format specifier to the `printf` function along with the corresponding value. A *format specifier* is a placeholder in the format string: a `%` followed by a letter that tells `printf` how to show the next value. For example, printing an integer requires the integer format specifier (`%d`), while printing a character requires the character format specifier (`%c`). This concept can be demonstrated using the following C code:

The format specifier informs `printf` how the provided data should be interpreted and displayed. Assembly works the same way: give `printf` the right format specifier and put the value in the right register.

## The big picture

Just like printing strings, printing other data types in AArch64 assembly uses the `printf` function. The general process is:

1. Define a format string containing the appropriate format specifier.
2. Load the address of the format string into `x0`.
3. Place the value to be printed into the next argument register.
4. Call `printf`.
The example below demonstrates how to use `printf` in assembly to print both an integer and a character. In this example, the program prints the integer 67 and the character L.

## Defining the format string

The first step in printing an integer and a character is to define format strings containing the appropriate format specifiers. Since we are printing both an integer and a character, we need the `%d` format specifier for the integer and the `%c` format specifier for the character.

This can be achieved by declaring two string variables in the `.data` section. The following code demonstrates this process:

body.source:
.data
fmt_int:    .string "Integer: %d\n"        // for printing an integer
fmt_char:   .string "Character: %c\n"      // for printing a character

body.markdown: In the above code, the variable `fmt_int` serves as the format string for printing an integer using the `%d` format specifier. Similarly, the variable `fmt_char` serves as the format string for printing a character using the `%c` format specifier. Both strings are defined using the `.string` directive.
You can print other data types in assembly by defining a format string with the matching format specifier. The specifiers are the same ones C uses; the table further down lists the common ones.

## Loading the format string address

Loading the format string address is done in the same way as loading the address of a string variable when printing a string. The `ldr` instruction loads the address of the format string into `x0`.

The following code demonstrates the process of loading the format string address:

body.source:
ldr     x0, =fmt_int                // before the first call

        ldr     x0, =fmt_char               // before the second call

body.markdown: In the code above, the address of each format string is loaded into `x0`: `fmt_int` for the integer and `fmt_char` for the character. Each one is loaded just before its own `printf` call, because the integer and the character are printed with different format strings.

The format string is always loaded into the first argument register (`x0`) before calling `printf`, regardless of the data type being printed. This is because `printf` expects the format string to be passed as its first argument.

The corresponding values are then passed in the next argument registers (`x1`, `x2`, and so on). If the format string contains multiple format specifiers, the values must be passed in the order they appear in the format string.

Floating-point values are the exception. They travel in the floating-point registers, which are counted separately, so the first one goes in `d0` even when `x1` already holds an integer. `printf` always receives a floating-point value as a 64-bit double, so a 32-bit float in `s0` must be widened first with `fcvt d0, s0`. The [floating-point lesson](/learn/floating-point) covers this.

## Passing the values to print

The corresponding values are passed by placing them in the next available argument register. The format string already fills `x0`, so the next one is `x1`: the integer value `67` and the character `L` are each placed in `w1` before their respective `printf` calls. `w1` is the 32-bit view of `x1`, and it is the right size here because `%d` and `%c` both read a 32-bit `int`.

`'L'` is a *character constant*: the assembler replaces it with the character's code in ASCII, the standard table that gives each character a number. The code for `L` is 76, and `%c` prints the character whose code the register holds.

The following code demonstrates how values are passed to the format string:

body.source:
ldr     x0, =fmt_int
        mov     w1, 67

        ldr     x0, =fmt_char
        mov     w1, 'L'

body.markdown: In the code above, the integer value `67` and the character `L` are placed in `w1` before their respective `printf` calls.

## Calling printf

Once all the required arguments have been set up correctly, the final step is to call the `printf` function with the `bl` instruction. The following code demonstrates how to call the `printf` function:

body.source:
ldr     x0, =fmt_int
        mov     w1, 67
        bl      printf

        ldr     x0, =fmt_char
        mov     w1, 'L'
        bl      printf

body.markdown: Notice that `x0` and `w1` are both set again before the second call. `printf` is allowed to change any of `x0` to `x18`, so neither value is guaranteed to survive the first call.
In assembly you call any function with `bl` followed by the function name.

## The whole program

The following program prints an integer and a character using `printf`. It prints `Integer: 67` on the first line and `Character: L` on the second.

Change the `%d` in `fmt_int` to `%c` and run it again. The first line becomes `Integer: C`, because 67 is the code for the letter C: the specifier, not the register, decides how a value is shown.

body.starter:
// Print an integer with %d and a character with %c

define(fp, x29)
define(lr, x30)

.data
fmt_int:    .string "Integer: %d\n"
fmt_char:   .string "Character: %c\n"

.text
        .balign 4
        .global main
main:
        stp     fp, lr, [sp, -16]!
        mov     fp, sp

        ldr     x0, =fmt_int                // x0 holds the format string
        mov     w1, 67                      // w1 holds the value it formats
        bl      printf

        ldr     x0, =fmt_char               // printf may have changed x0 and w1,
        mov     w1, 'L'                     // so both are set again
        bl      printf

        mov     w0, 0
        ldp     fp, lr, [sp], 16
        ret

body.markdown:
## Matching the specifier to the register width

Each specifier also says how wide its value is, and the register you fill has to match. `%d` reads a 32-bit `int`, so it takes a `w` register; `%ld` reads a 64-bit `long`, so it takes an `x` register.

| Specifier | Prints | Fill |
|---|---|---|
| `%d` | a signed integer in decimal | a `w` register |
| `%u` | an unsigned integer in decimal | a `w` register |
| `%x` | an integer in hexadecimal | a `w` register |
| `%c` | the character with that code | a `w` register |
| `%ld` | a 64-bit signed integer in decimal | an `x` register |
| `%lx` | a 64-bit integer in hexadecimal | an `x` register |
| `%s` | the string at that address | an `x` register holding an address |
| `%f` | a double | a `d` register |

When the widths disagree, `printf` reads the wrong number of bits. With 5000000000 in `x1`, `%ld` prints 5000000000, but `%d` reads only the low 32 bits and prints 705032704.

## Several values in one call

One format string can hold several specifiers. `printf` fills them from left to right: the first specifier takes `w1`, the second `w2`, the third `w3`, and so on up to `x7`. Values past the seventh go on the stack, which a later lesson covers.

The program below prints `Seat B12 costs 45 dollars.` from a single call. Swap the numbers in `w2` and `w3` and run it again: the line becomes `Seat B45 costs 12 dollars.`, because `printf` matches values to specifiers by position alone.

body.starter:
// One printf with three specifiers, filled from w1, w2 and w3 in order

define(fp, x29)
define(lr, x30)

.data
fmt_seat:   .string "Seat %c%d costs %d dollars.\n"

.text
        .balign 4
        .global main
main:
        stp     fp, lr, [sp, -16]!
        mov     fp, sp

        ldr     x0, =fmt_seat
        mov     w1, 'B'                     // first specifier, %c
        mov     w2, 12                      // second, %d
        mov     w3, 45                      // third, %d
        bl      printf

        mov     w0, 0
        ldp     fp, lr, [sp], 16
        ret

body.markdown:
## Check yourself

1. A format string holds two specifiers. Which registers carry their values?
2. You want to print the 64-bit value in `x19`. Which specifier do you use, and which register do you fill?
3. What does `mov w1, 'A'` put in `w1`, and what do `%d` and `%c` print for it?

Answers:

1. `w1` (or `x1`) for the first and `w2` (or `x2`) for the second; the format string itself is in `x0`.
2. `%ld`, with `mov x1, x19`.
3. 65, the code for A: `%d` prints 65 and `%c` prints A.
